content_voiceover: This flowchart addresses first line therapy for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma patients who are not transplant candidates. Treatment choice depends on insurance coverage rules, patient preference, comorbidities, renal function, neurologic status, hematopoietic reserve, tumor aggressiveness, presence of extramedullary disease, and physician preference. Options are organized by number of drug classes combined, quadruplet, triplet, or doublet regimens. Among quadruplets, daratumumab VMP and VMPT exist, though VMPT isn't considered mainstream. For triplets, the combination of a proteasome inhibitor plus an immunomodulatory drug, currently the mainstream first line approach, includes VRd, RVD-lite for frailer patients, and VTD. Proteasome inhibitor only triplets include VCD and VMP. Immunomodulatory drug based triplets include daratumumab-Rd as an option, while CTd, CRd, MPT, and MPR are non-mainstream alternatives used in select situations. Doublets split into proteasome inhibitor based, such as VD, or immunomodulatory drug based, such as Rd or TD. The NCCN table on this slide echoes this hierarchy, with the preferred category one regimens being daratumumab-lenalidomide-dexamethasone, daratumumab-bortezomib-lenalidomide-dexamethasone for non-frail patients under eighty, and isatuximab-bortezomib-lenalidomide-dexamethasone under similar criteria.
keypoints: Non-transplant first line therapy is chosen based on comorbidities and frailty
PI plus IMiD triplets like VRd are the current first line mainstream
Quadruplets like daratumumab VMP exist but VMPT is not mainstream
NCCN preferred regimens are Dara-Rd, Dara-VRd, and Isa-VRd, category 1
Doublets such as VD or Rd are reserved for frailer or less aggressive disease
keypoint_voiceover: Key takeaway here, PI plus IMiD triplets such as VRd represent the current mainstream first line approach for transplant ineligible patients, and NCCN ranks daratumumab or isatuximab based quadruplets as preferred category one options for appropriately selected patients, while doublets are reserved for frail patients.
